opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important asymmetries to watch. The way I'd frame it is that AI systems get good at things roughly in proportion to how cheap, fast, and unambiguous the feedback is. Coding is the canonical example: you write the code, you run the tests, you know within seconds whether it worked. That's why we've seen such rapid progress there. Math with formal verification is similar.

Idea generation is interesting because it sits in a weird spot. In some sense, generating a candidate idea is cheap, and models are already quite good at producing lots of plausible-sounding hypotheses, research directions, product concepts. But knowing whether an idea is *good* often requires a long, expensive process downstream. Did this research direction pan out after two years? Did this startup idea actually find product-market fit? That signal is slow and noisy, and it's confounded by execution. So I expect models to get very good at the "breadth" part of ideation, generating a big menu, and somewhat slower at the "taste" part, picking which idea is actually worth pursuing, except in domains where you can quickly test ideas, like ML experiments that run in an afternoon.

Long-horizon execution is, I think, even harder from a feedback standpoint, at least naively. If a task takes a month, you get one data point per month per attempt, and when it fails, credit assignment is brutal. Was it the plan, or step 37, or the environment changing? So you can't just brute-force reinforcement learning on month-long tasks the way you can on ten-second tasks.

But here's where I think people sometimes underrate progress: long tasks are often decomposable into chains of shorter tasks with their own local feedback. A lot of what it means to be good at a long project is being reliable at the short steps, noticing when you've gone off track, and recovering. Those skills can be trained on shorter horizons and then compose. We've seen the length of tasks models can complete autonomously growing pretty steadily, and I think much of that comes from reliability and error-correction improving rather than models learning "month-long planning" directly.

So my overall expectation is: fast progress wherever the loop is tight, which increasingly includes AI research itself, since a lot of it is run-the-experiment, look-at-the-number. Slower progress on judgment-heavy, slow-feedback stuff like strategic taste or navigating messy real-world institutions. And the big wildcard is whether AI systems start generating their own feedback well, acting as good critics and simulators of outcomes. If they can, that closes a lot of the gap, and that's the scenario where I think things could move a lot faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response says AI improves fastest where feedback is cheap, fast, and clear, using coding and formal math as examples.

r002.rationale: It says running code tests gives quick feedback on whether the code worked, but does not identify that signal as hard to fake.

r003.rationale: It contrasts generating ideas with long-horizon execution, but does not state that training plans people judge favorably is easier than training execution of a year-long plan.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing to notice is that "generating ideas" and "executing long-term plans" are actually very different in terms of how easy it is to get a clean training signal.

For idea generation, the loop is tight. You can ask a model for a hundred research directions or a hundred candidate explanations, and a human, or increasingly another model, can look at them and say "this one is interesting, that one is dumb." The feedback comes fast, it's cheap, and you can generate a lot of it. So I expect models to get very good at that quite quickly, and honestly they already are. They're well-read, they combine things across fields, and they'll throw out suggestions that a human expert wouldn't have thought of.

Long-horizon execution is harder precisely because the feedback is sparse and delayed. If the task is "run this research program for six months and come back with a result," you only get one bit of signal at the end, and that bit is tangled up with a thousand decisions made along the way. It's much harder to know which step was the mistake. Historically that's why models have been impressive in short bursts but kind of flaky when you leave them alone for a long time: they drift, they lose the thread, they don't notice when something has gone wrong.

But I don't think that's a fixed ceiling. What's happening now is that labs are building environments where you can get intermediate signal on agentic tasks: did the code compile, did the tests pass, did the subgoal get achieved. Once you can decompose a long task into checkable chunks, you can train on it, and the horizon the models can handle starts stretching. We've seen that length roughly doubling on a fairly regular cadence, and I don't see a strong reason that stops.

So my expectation is a lag rather than a permanent gap. Idea generation gets good first, because the feedback loop is naturally fast. Execution catches up a bit later, as people invest in making the loop faster for it. And the thing I'd watch for is the moment when models are good enough at execution that they can run the experiments to evaluate their own ideas. At that point the two capabilities start feeding each other, and that's when I'd expect things to accelerate in a way that feels qualitatively different.

r001.rationale: It says idea generation has fast, cheap feedback and should improve quickly, while long-horizon execution has sparse, delayed feedback.

r002.rationale: It names code compiling and tests passing as intermediate signals, but does not identify whether code that runs is a hard-to-fake training signal.

r003.rationale: It contrasts easy evaluation of research ideas with executing a six-month research program, but does not state that generating favorably judged plans is easier than executing a year-long plan.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is how quickly you can tell whether something worked. If an AI is generating ideas, and you can test those ideas cheaply and get feedback in minutes or hours, you can get a really powerful loop: generate a bunch of possibilities, try them, learn from the results, and generate better ones. You don’t necessarily need the system to be great at managing a whole project for that to be useful.

With long-term plans, the feedback can be much harder to interpret. If you make a decision today and the project fails six months from now, which decision was responsible? Was the plan bad, or was the execution bad, or did something unexpected happen? That makes it harder to improve through trial and error.

So I’d expect progress to be uneven. You could have systems that produce very impressive ideas in domains where there’s a good way to evaluate them, while still being unreliable at carrying out a long, messy project. But those capabilities aren’t completely separate. If you can break a project into smaller pieces with useful feedback along the way, you can make long-term execution more tractable. A lot turns on whether those intermediate signals actually tell you that you’re making progress toward the ultimate goal.

r001.rationale: It says ideas can improve through a powerful loop when they can be tested cheaply and quickly, and contrasts this with unreliable long-term execution.

r002.rationale: It does not mention generated code running as a hard-to-fake training signal.

r003.rationale: It contrasts idea generation with long-term execution, but does not say that training AI to produce plans people judge favorably is easier than training it to execute a year-long plan.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is how quickly you can tell whether something worked. If an AI generates an idea for an experiment or a piece of code, and you can test it immediately, you get this very powerful loop: try something, get feedback, improve. You could see really rapid progress in domains where that feedback is cheap and reliable.

With long-term plans, the feedback is often much worse. If you’re trying to run an organization or pursue a research agenda over several years, you don’t necessarily know whether you made a good decision until much later. And even then, it can be hard to tell whether the outcome reflects your decision or just luck. So being very good at generating plausible ideas doesn’t automatically imply being very good at carrying out those plans.

But I wouldn’t treat that as a permanent barrier. Part of good planning is breaking a big goal into smaller steps where you can get feedback along the way. To the extent that AI systems learn to do that, they could become much better at long-term execution too. I’d expect progress to be uneven, with the fastest improvement where there are clear tests of success.

r001.rationale: It says rapid improvement is likely where feedback is quick and reliable, and progress fastest where success has clear tests.

r002.rationale: It mentions testing generated code immediately, but does not identify whether code running is a hard-to-fake training signal.

r003.rationale: It contrasts generating plausible ideas with carrying out plans over several years, but does not state that training AI to generate favorably judged plans is easier than training it to execute a year-long plan.
